narrativeProgression.description: The speaker introduces Aaron Swartz, a friend he met at Stanford in 2005.
Aaron posted a humorous account of searching for the speaker's 'ghostly presence' at Stanford.
Aaron had to choose between attending the speaker's talk and taking a final exam. He did both.
The speaker and Aaron would meet over the years, with the speaker providing reading lists for Aaron.
Two years ago, Aaron told the speaker about downloading 4.5 million scholarly articles.
The speaker questioned why MIT wasn't celebrating Aaron's achievement.
The speaker told Aaron that only a small fraction of the articles were worth reading.
The speaker suggested Aaron needed a quality control mechanism to filter the downloaded articles.
The speaker suggested Aaron link his downloads to a citation index to focus on highly cited articles.
The speaker shared a personal story about his own illegal hacking experience as a student.
The speaker recounted his involvement in building a 'blue box' for free long-distance phone calls in 1962.
The speaker and his housemate achieved the 'longest long-distance phone call ever made,' from Palo Alto to New York via Hawaii.
AT&T tapped the speaker's phone during their experiment.
The speaker received a call from AT&T's head of security, A.J. Dodge, who informed him that their actions were a crime.
The speaker knew the situation wasn't serious because Dodge cared about the engineering aspect.
The speaker was told to stop the hacking and turn over his equipment to AT&T.
The speaker expressed gratitude to Dodge and AT&T for not ruining his life.
The speaker highlighted Aaron's unique quality of being 'marvelously and vigorously different.'

climax.description: The speaker's reflection on Aaron's unique quality and the need for more people to be different serves as the emotional climax of the speech.
